claims.claim: E. coli does not exhibit DddA-mediated inhibition when grown in competition with B. cenocepacia.
claims.source: Surprisingly, we found no evidence of DddA-mediated inhibition of E. coli in these experiments.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through bacterial competition assays shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: A B. cenocepacia strain lacking T6SS-1 activity (∆icmF) exhibits reduced competitiveness toward E. coli.
claims.source: However, we observed that a B. cenocepacia strain lacking T6SS-1 activity (∆icmF) exhibits reduced competitiveness toward E. coli, indicating that toxin delivery can occur between these organisms.
claims.evidence: This is shown through competition assays in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: The effect of DddA delivery via T6SS varies among different Gram-negative organisms.
claims.source: We found that the effect of DddA delivery via the T6SS varied; in general, enteric species and Acinetobacter baumannii (Figure 3A and B) resisted intoxication, whereas other species, including Pseudomonas aeruginosa, P. putida, and other Burkholderia species (Figure 3C and D), were highly sensitive to DddA-mediated killing.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through competition assays shown in Figure 3A-D.

claims.claim: E. coli populations subject to intoxication by T6SS-1 of wild-type B. cenocepacia for a single hour display a nearly 10-fold increase in the frequency of rifampicin-resistant cells compared to those exposed to B. cenocepacia dddAE1347A.
claims.source: Strikingly, we found that E. coli populations subject to intoxication by T6SS-1 of wild-type B. cenocepacia for a single hour display a nearly 10-fold increase in the frequency of rifampicin-resistant (RifR) cells compared to those exposed to B. cenocepacia dddAE1347A (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This is shown through mutation frequency measurements in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: In 24 of 25 rifampicin-resistant E. coli clones from competition with B. cenocepacia, resistance was conferred by C•G-to-T•A transitions within the preferred context of DddA.
claims.source: Sequencing of rpoB from 25 independent clones obtained from E. coli populations grown in competition with B. cenocepacia revealed that in all but one of these, rifampicin resistance was conferred by C•G-to-T•A transitions within the preferred context of DddA (Figure 4B, Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This is shown through rpoB sequencing data in Figure 4B and Supplementary file 1.

claims.claim: There is significant enrichment for C•G-to-T•A transitions in the 5′-TC-3′ context in rpoB of DddA-intoxicated E. coli populations compared to spontaneous RifR mutants.
claims.source: In contrast, a study of 152 spontaneous RifR mutants in E. coli found only 32 such mutations in rpoB (Garibyan et al., 2003), indicating significant enrichment for this sequence signature in clones deriving from DddA-intoxicated populations (Fisher's exact test, p<0.001).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through statistical comparison with published data from Garibyan et al., 2003.

claims.claim: Whole-genome sequencing of 10 RifR E. coli clones revealed 12 additional mutations outside of rpoB, all of which were C•G-to-T•A transitions in a 5′-TC-3′ context.
claims.source: Whole-genome sequencing (WGS) of 10 RifR clones isolated from these experiments led to the identification of an additional 12 mutations outside of rpoB distributed across these strains, and all were C•G-to-T•A transitions in a 5′-TC-3′ context (Figure 4B and C, Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This is shown through whole genome sequencing data in Figure 4B-C and Supplementary file 1.

claims.claim: K. pneumoniae and enterohemorrhagic E. coli (EHEC) display higher RifR frequency when in contact with B. cenocepacia containing active DddA than with B. cenocepacia bearing the dddAE1347A allele.
claims.source: Among the resistant organisms, Klebsiella pneumoniae and enterohemorrhagic E. coli (EHEC) displayed higher RifR frequency when in contact with B. cenocepacia containing active DddA than when in contact with B. cenocepacia bearing the dddAE1347A allele (Figure 4D and E)
claims.evidence: This is shown through mutation frequency measurements in Figure 4D and E.

claims.claim: Within 11 K. pneumoniae isolates sequenced, 50 of 51 SNPs detected were C•G-to-T•A transitions in the 5′-TC-3′ context preferred by DddA.
claims.source: Within the 11 K. pneumoniae isolates we sequenced, 50 of the 51 SNPs detected were C•G-to-T•A transitions, and each of these was located in the 5′-TC-3′ context preferred by DddA (Mok et al., 2020), a highly significant enrichment compared to spontaneous mutation patterns (p<0.001) (Lee et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is shown through whole genome sequencing data with statistical analysis comparing to spontaneous mutation patterns from Lee et al., 2012.

claims.claim: In EHEC isolates, 82 of 88 SNPs across seven strains corresponded to C•G-to-T•A transitions in the context preferred by DddA.
claims.source: The EHEC isolates we sequenced shared this trend, with 82 of 88 SNPs across seven strains corresponding to C•G-to-T•A transitions in the context preferred by DddA.
claims.evidence: This is shown through whole genome sequencing data in Figure 4H-I and Supplementary file 1.

claims.claim: There is no indication of clustering of DddA-induced mutations across genomes of E. coli, K. pneumoniae, or EHEC.
claims.source: We found no indication of clustering of DddA-induced mutations across genomes of E. coli, K. pneumoniae, or EHEC, suggesting that mutagenesis by the toxin occurs in a random fashion (Figure 4C,F and I).
claims.evidence: This is shown through genome distribution plots in Figure 4C, F, and I.

claims.claim: There is no evidence of increased mutation frequency in populations of B. cenocepacia K56-2, B. ambifaria, and P. aeruginosa that are susceptible to DddA killing.
claims.source: We observed no evidence of increased mutation frequency in populations of the susceptible competitors B. cenocepacia K56-2, B. ambifaria, and P. aeruginosa (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–E).
claims.evidence: This is shown through mutation frequency measurements in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C-E.

claims.claim: Intoxication of P. aeruginosa ∆ung by DddA yields elevated mutation frequency, resembling that of Enterobacteriaceae exposed to the toxin.
claims.source: However, intoxication of P. aeruginosa ∆ung by DddA yielded elevated mutation frequency, resembling that of Enterobacteriaceae exposed to the toxin (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
claims.evidence: This is shown through mutation frequency measurements in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F.

claims.claim: Eight deaminase superfamily subfamilies possess members associated with interbacterial toxin systems.
claims.source: Aravind and colleagues describe 22 sequence divergent subfamilies into which enzymes belonging to the deaminase superfamily distribute (Iyer et al., 2011). Among these, eight subfamilies possess members associated with interbacterial toxin systems (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analysis from Iyer et al., 2011 and shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: P. syringae WP_011168804.1 (BaDTF2) and T. equigenitalis WP_044956253.1 (BaDTF3) exhibit toxicity when heterologously expressed in E. coli.
claims.source: Like DddA, both exhibited toxicity when heterologously expressed in E. coli (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This is shown through toxicity assays in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: BaDTF2 and BaDTF3 representatives introduce high levels of C•G-to-T•A transitions when expressed in E. coli.
claims.source: Remarkably, despite their sequence divergence from DddA, representatives from both BaDTF2 and BaDTF3 introduced high levels of C•G-to-T•A transitions (Figure 5C–F).
claims.evidence: This is shown through SNV analysis in Figure 5C-F.

claims.claim: The BaDTF2 representative preferentially targets cytosine within pyrimidine tracks (5'-YCY) but can also deaminate cytosines in all other contexts with lower efficiency.
claims.source: The BaDTF2 representative preferentially targeted cytosine located within pyrimidine tracks (5'-YCY), but could also deaminate cytosines in all other contexts with lower efficiency (Figure 5G).
claims.evidence: This is shown through sequence logo analysis in Figure 5G.

claims.claim: The BaDTF3 member targets cytosine most efficiently when preceded by thymidine, and less efficiently when preceded by adenosine or cytosine; it does not act on cytosines preceded by guanosine (5'-HC).
claims.source: In contrast, the BaDTF3 member targeted cytosine most efficiently when preceded by thymidine, and less efficiently when preceded by adenosine or cytosine; it did not act on cytosines preceded by guanosine (5'-HC) (Figure 5H).
claims.evidence: This is shown through sequence logo analysis in Figure 5H.

claims.claim: The BaDTF2 protein (SsdA) exhibits potent cytosine deaminating activity toward single-stranded DNA.
claims.source: Unlike DddA, the BaDTF2 protein exhibited potent cytosine deaminating activity toward ssDNA (Figure 5I).
claims.evidence: This is shown through in vitro deamination assays in Figure 5I.

claims.claim: SsdA targets cytosine residues in double-stranded DNA with considerably lower efficiency than single-stranded DNA.
claims.source: Cytosine residues in dsDNA were also targeted, but with considerably lower efficiency (Figure 5J).
claims.evidence: This is shown through in vitro deamination assays in Figure 5J.

claims.claim: Purified SsdAtox can target cytosine residues preceded by any of the four bases.
claims.source: Consistent with the in vivo mutagenesis results, purified SsdAtox could target cytosine residues preceded by any of the four bases (Figure 5K).
claims.evidence: This is shown through in vitro deamination assays in Figure 5K.

claims.claim: SsdAtox exhibits only residual activity toward RNA targets in vitro.
claims.source: Notably, we detected only residual activity of SsdAtox toward RNA targets in vitro, suggesting that DNA is the physiologically relevant substrate of the toxin (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is shown through poisoned primer extension assays in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: RNA-seq analysis of E. coli cells expressing SsdAtox revealed no detectable increase in the number of C•G-to-T•A transitions in cDNA sequences.
claims.source: This is supported by RNA-seq analysis of E. coli cells expressing SddAtox, which revealed no detectable increase in the number of C•G-to-T•A transitions in cDNA sequences (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and C).
claims.evidence: This is shown through RNA-seq analysis in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and C.

claims.claim: The structure of SsdA in complex with SsdAI was determined to 3.0 Å resolution.
claims.source: To begin to understand the basis for the distinct substrate preference exhibited by SsdA, we determined its structure in complex with its immunity determinant, SsdAI, to 3.0 Å (Figure 6A and Supplementary file 2).
claims.evidence: This is stated directly and shown in Figure 6A with crystallographic data in Supplementary file 2.

claims.claim: The structure of SsdA exhibits the basic characteristics of deaminase enzymes, including active site histidine and cysteine residues in position to coordinate a zinc ion.
claims.source: The structure of SsdA exhibits the basic characteristics of deaminase enzymes, including active site histidine and cysteine residues in position to coordinate a zinc ion, and the five β-strands (S1-5) and three α-helices (H1, H3, and H4) that constitute the core fold of deaminase superfamily enzymes (Figure 6B; Iyer et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is shown through structural analysis in Figure 6B with reference to Iyer et al., 2011.

claims.claim: SsdA groups with the C-terminal hairpin division of the deaminase superfamily.
claims.source: More specifically, SsdA groups with the C-terminal hairpin division of the superfamily, and consistent with this assignment, S4 and S5 of SsdA are antiparallel.
claims.evidence: This is based on structural analysis and comparison with deaminase superfamily classification from Iyer et al., 2011.

claims.claim: SsdA bears little structural homology with characterized deaminases, including DddA.
claims.source: Outside of its basic fold, SsdA bears little structural homology with characterized deaminases, including DddA (Figure 6C–E).
claims.evidence: This is shown through structural comparison in Figure 6C-E.

claims.claim: SsdA bears most overall structural similarity with the folate-dependent transformylase domain of PurH (DALI Z score, 7.7).
claims.source: Indeed, SsdA bears most overall structural similarity with the folate-dependent transformylase domain of PurH (DALI; Z score, 7.7), which contains the deaminase fold despite its sequence and functional divergence from deaminase enzymes (Iyer et al., 2011; Wolan et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: This is based on DALI structural comparison analysis with references to Iyer et al., 2011 and Wolan et al., 2002.

claims.claim: SsdAI is an exclusively α-helical protein that shares a large (~1300 Å2) interface with SsdA.
claims.source: SsdAI is an exclusively α-helical protein that shares a large (~1300 Å2) interface with SsdA.
claims.evidence: This is determined from the crystal structure shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: The SsdA-interacting surface of SsdAI effectively demarcates the active site of SsdA.
claims.source: As is often observed in toxin–immunity co-crystal structures, this interface effectively demarcates the active site of SsdA (Figure 6A; Hernandez et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is shown in the structure in Figure 6A with reference to general principles from Hernandez et al., 2020.

claims.claim: SsdAI residues contact a conserved Ser-Gly-Trp (SGW) motif that resides in close proximity to the active site of SsdA and is unique to the BaDTF2 members of the DYW subgroup.
claims.source: Interestingly, these residues contact a conserved Ser-Gly-Trp (SGW) motif that resides in close proximity to the active site of SsdA and is unique to the BaDTF2 members of the DYW subgroup.
claims.evidence: This is shown through structural analysis in Figure 6D and F, and sequence analysis in Figure 6G.

claims.claim: Several conserved features of DYW proteins important for mitochondrial or chloroplast gene editing in vivo are absent from BaDTF2 proteins.
claims.source: Our search revealed several conserved features of DYW proteins previously demonstrated to be important for mitochondrial or chloroplast gene editing in vivo that are absent from the BaDTF2 proteins. These include the eponymous C-terminal DYW residues, a CxC motif believed to be important for coordinating a second Zn2+ atom, and a proline-glycine (PG) motif located within a characteristic insertion between S2 and H2 of the deaminase fold (Figure 6G; Boussardon et al., 2014; Gutmann et al., 2020; Wagoner et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is shown through sequence analysis in Figure 6G with references to Boussardon et al., 2014; Gutmann et al., 2020; Wagoner et al., 2015.

claims.claim: BaDTF2 proteins contain a conserved SGW motif within the insertion between S2 and H2 of the deaminase fold, instead of the PG motif found in DYW proteins.
claims.source: Instead, BaDTF2 proteins contain the aforementioned SGW motif within this insertion.
claims.evidence: This is shown through sequence analysis in Figure 6G.

claims.claim: DddA is a double-stranded DNA-targeting cytosine deaminase.
claims.source: We recently demonstrated that one of these proteins, a substrate of an interbacterial toxin-delivering T6SS of Burkholderia cenocepacia, acts as a double-stranded DNA-targeting cytosine deaminase (Mok et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is stated with reference to prior work from Mok et al., 2020.

claims.claim: DddA's activity of targeting double-stranded DNA stands in contrast with all previously characterized DNA-targeting deaminases, which act preferentially on single-stranded substrates.
claims.source: This unusual activity stands in contrast with all previously characterized DNA-targeting deaminases, which act preferentially on single-stranded substrates.
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about previously characterized deaminases.

claims.claim: DddA is highly toxic when expressed heterologously in E. coli.
claims.source: We also showed that unlike the housekeeping deaminases APOBEC3G, TadA, and Cdd, this protein, which we named DddA (double-stranded DNA deaminase A), is highly toxic when expressed heterologously in Escherichia coli.
claims.evidence: This is stated with reference to prior work from Mok et al., 2020.

claims.claim: Cytosine deamination generates uracil, which is removed from DNA by the base excision repair (BER) pathway.
claims.source: Cytosine deamination generates uracil, which is removed from DNA by the base excision repair (BER) pathway (Wallace, 2014).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Wallace, 2014.

claims.claim: The presence of abasic sites in close proximity on opposite DNA strands can lead to double-strand DNA breaks.
claims.source: This process generates abasic sites and previous reports indicate that the presence of these lesions in close proximity on opposite strands can lead to double-strand DNA breaks (D'souza and Harrison, 2003).
claims.evidence: This is cited from D'souza and Harrison, 2003.

claims.claim: Pathways for the delivery of toxins into contacting cells are widespread in bacteria.
claims.source: Pathways for the delivery of toxins into contacting cells are widespread in bacteria. These include the type IV-VI secretion systems (T4-T6SS) in Gram-negative bacteria, the Esx secretion system of Gram-positives, and a number of specialized mechanisms that display a more limited distribution (Klein et al., 2020; García-Bayona et al., 2017; Jamet et al., 2015; Koskiniemi et al., 2013; Vassallo et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge cited from multiple references.

claims.claim: Within populations of toxin-producing strains, self-intoxication is prevented through the production of specific immunity determinants that neutralize individual toxins.
claims.source: Within populations of toxin-producing strains, self-intoxication is prevented through the production of specific immunity determinants that neutralize individual toxins (Hernandez et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Hernandez et al., 2020.

claims.claim: In Burkholderia thailandensis, a CDI toxin causes increased expression of more than 30 genes in resistant cells, including those encoding exopolysaccharide biosynthesis proteins and a T6SS.
claims.source: However, in Burkholderia thailandensis, it was demonstrated that a toxin delivered by the contact-dependent inhibition pathway (CDI) causes increased expression of more than 30 genes in resistant cells, including those encoding exopolysaccharide biosynthesis proteins and a T6SS (Garcia et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is cited from Garcia et al., 2016.

claims.claim: Within a population of CDI toxin-producing bacteria, some cells fail to completely neutralize incoming CDI toxins, leading to induction of the stringent response and enhanced antibiotic tolerance via growth arrest.
claims.source: A separate study found that within a population of CDI toxin-producing bacteria, some cells fail to completely neutralize incoming CDI toxins delivered by their neighbors, leading to induction of the stringent response, and ultimately to enhanced antibiotic tolerance via growth arrest of this sub-population (Ghosh et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is cited from Ghosh et al., 2018.

claims.claim: Whether toxin delivery can impact the long-term evolutionary landscape of target cell populations has not been explored.
claims.source: Whether toxin delivery can impact the long-term evolutionary landscape of target cell populations has not been explored.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge that the current study addresses.

claims.claim: Proteins that catalyze the deamination of bases in nucleotides and nucleic acids are found in all domains of life and play essential roles in a range of physiological functions.
claims.source: Proteins that catalyze the deamination of bases in nucleotides and nucleic acids are found in all domains of life and play essential roles in a range of physiological functions (Iyer et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Iyer et al., 2011.

claims.claim: Bioinformatic analyses revealed that a large and diverse collection of predicted bacterial and archaeal deaminases exhibit hallmarks of substrates of antibacterial toxin delivery pathways.
claims.source: Bioinformatic analyses of the origins of the deaminase fold led to the surprising finding that a large and diverse collection of predicted bacterial and archaeal deaminases exhibit hallmarks of substrates of antibacterial toxin delivery pathways, including the T6SS, the Esx secretion system, and the CDI pathway (Iyer et al., 2004; Makarova et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is cited from Iyer et al., 2004 and Makarova et al., 2019.

claims.claim: dddA is encoded in only 97 of 308 B. cenocepacia strains with publicly available genomes.
claims.source: Given that dddA is encoded in only 97 of 308 B. cenocepacia strains with publicly available genomes and is missing from widely employed model strains of this species (J2315 and K56-2), we also evaluated whether it could mediate intoxication of a strain lacking the effector gene and its accompanying immunity determinant, dddAI.
claims.evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analysis of publicly available genomes.

claims.claim: B. cenocepacia K56-2 was susceptible to DddA intoxication to a level similar to other Burkholderia species tested.
claims.source: We found that this strain, B. cenocepacia K56-2, was susceptible to intoxication to a level similar to other Burkholderia species tested (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: This is shown through competition assays in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: In all sensitive bacteria tested, DddA accounted for all the inhibitory activity of the T6SS of B. cenocepacia under the conditions of the assay.
claims.source: Notably, in all the sensitive bacteria, DddA accounted for all the inhibitory activity of the T6SS of B. cenocepacia under the conditions of our assay.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from competition assays shown in Figure 3C-D where dddAE1347A mutant shows no inhibitory activity.

claims.claim: The susceptibility of P. aeruginosa to DddA intoxication was not influenced by ung inactivation.
claims.source: Interestingly, the susceptibility of P. aeruginosa to DddA intoxication was not influenced by ung inactivation (Figure 3G), consistent with our earlier conclusion that cell death mediated by the toxin occurs upstream of massive uracil accumulation and widespread chromosome fragmentation (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: This is shown through viability assays in Figure 3G.

claims.claim: Salmonella enterica and Acinetobacter baumannii did not exhibit increased RifR frequency when exposed to B. cenocepacia with active DddA.
claims.source: Among the resistant organisms, Klebsiella pneumoniae and enterohemorrhagic E. coli (EHEC) displayed higher RifR frequency when in contact with B. cenocepacia containing active DddA than when in contact with B. cenocepacia bearing the dddAE1347A allele (Figure 4D and E); Salmonella enterica and Acinetobacter baumanii did not exhibit this behavior (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B).
claims.evidence: This is shown through mutation frequency measurements in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B.

claims.claim: The genomes of 65 RifR P. aeruginosa clones derived from interbacterial growth competition experiments revealed mutations exclusively within rpoB, with only 15% conforming to the mutagenic signature of DddA.
claims.source: Furthermore, the genomes of 65 RifR P. aeruginosa clones derived from interbacterial growth competition experiments between P. aeruginosa and B. cenocepacia revealed mutations exclusively within rpoB, and only 15% of these mutations conformed to the mutagenic signature of DddA (Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This is shown through whole genome sequencing data in Supplementary file 1.

claims.claim: Mutagenesis is likely a rare outcome of DddA-mediated intoxication in sensitive competitor species.
claims.source: These results suggest that mutagenesis is likely a rare outcome of DddA-mediated intoxication in sensitive competitor species, but raise the possibility that it may become more frequent in strains unable to repair DddA-catalyzed lesions in DNA.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that susceptible species show little mutagenesis unless ung is deleted.

claims.claim: Previously characterized proteins in the DYW deaminase family are found in plants and protists and participate in C to U editing of specific organellar mRNA transcripts.
claims.source: Previously characterized proteins in the DYW deaminase family are found in plants and protists and participate in C to U editing of specific organellar mRNA transcripts (Hayes and Santibanez, 2017; Oldenkott et al., 2019; Shikanai, 1847).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Hayes and Santibanez, 2017; Oldenkott et al., 2019; Shikanai, 1847.

claims.claim: In DYW proteins from plants and protists, the DYW deaminase domain is generally found at the C-terminus of a larger polypeptide characterized by pentatricopeptide repeats (PPRs), which recruit the catalytic domain to target mRNAs.
claims.source: In these organisms, the DYW deaminase domain is generally found at the C-terminus of a larger polypeptide characterized by pentatricopeptide repeats (PPRs), which recruit the catalytic domain of the protein to target mRNAs (Barkan and Small, 2014).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Barkan and Small, 2014.

claims.claim: The structure of SsdA-SsdAI places the PG motif region in position to engage substrate.
claims.source: In this regard, our structure of the SsdA–SsdAI complex likely provides some insights. For example, it places the PG motif region, which differs markedly between BaDTF2 and DYW proteins, in position to engage substrate.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the crystal structure shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: DddA displays significantly greater structural relatedness to eukaryotic deaminases targeting ssDNA (AID/APOBEC) than it does to SsdA.
claims.source: Despite the predicted shared ancestry of DddA and SsdA, DddA displays significantly greater structural relatedness to eukaryotic deaminases targeting ssDNA (AID/APOBEC) than it does to SsdA.
claims.evidence: This is based on structural comparison analysis.

claims.claim: Cytosine deaminases targeting single-stranded DNA evolved at least twice from the ancestral deaminase fold.
claims.source: Taken together, this suggests that cytosine deaminases targeting ssDNA evolved at least twice from the ancestral deaminase fold (Iyer et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from structural comparisons with reference to Iyer et al., 2011.

claims.claim: The toxicity of SsdA could result from targeting highly transcribed genes that are more likely to exist in a single-stranded state.
claims.source: One explanation may be that because highly transcribed genes are more likely to exist in a single-stranded state, the toxicity of SsdA could result from the targeting of these specific regions.
claims.evidence: This is speculative reasoning about the mechanism of SsdA toxicity.

claims.claim: The lower level of dsDNA targeting by SsdA observed in vitro may represent the physiologically relevant activity of the protein during cellular intoxication.
claims.source: Alternatively, the lower level of dsDNA targeting by SsdA that we observe in vitro may represent the physiologically relevant activity of the protein during cellular intoxication.
claims.evidence: This is speculative reasoning about the mechanism of SsdA toxicity.

claims.claim: Thymine starvation leads to cell death in organisms from E. coli to humans, in a process known as thymineless death (TLD).
claims.source: While nutrient deprivation typically results in growth arrest, thymine starvation induced through genetic inactivation or chemical inhibition of thymine biosynthesis leads to cell death in organisms from E. coli to humans, in a process known as TLD (Khodursky et al., 2015; Hanawalt, 2015).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Khodursky et al., 2015 and Hanawalt, 2015.

claims.claim: Both TLD and DddA intoxication involve the incorporation of uracil into DNA and produce complex phenotypes including DNA replication arrest and chromosome degradation.
claims.source: There remains no consensus on the precise mechanism of TLD, but it is nevertheless possible to draw parallels between TLD and DddA intoxication. Both processes involve the incorporation of uracil into DNA and produce complex phenotypes including DNA replication arrest and chromosome degradation (Khodursky et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison with established knowledge about TLD from Khodursky et al., 2015.

claims.claim: For both TLD and DddA intoxication, the removal of uracil incorporated into DNA does not rescue cells from intoxication.
claims.source: Also, for both TLD and DddA intoxication, the removal of uracil incorporated into DNA does not rescue cells from intoxication (Sangurdekar et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2A and comparison with TLD literature from Sangurdekar et al., 2010.

claims.claim: Suppressor mutants resistant to killing by TLD appear to be difficult to obtain.
claims.source: More generally, suppressor mutants resistant to killing by TLD appear to be difficult to obtain (Fonville et al., 2011; Guzmán and Martín, 2015).
claims.evidence: This is cited from Fonville et al., 2011 and Guzmán and Martín, 2015.

claims.claim: The indelible signature that deaminase toxins leave within the genomes of target cells offers a unique opportunity to study bacterial interactions in nature.
claims.source: In this regard, the indelible signature that deaminase toxins leave within the genomes of target cells offers a unique opportunity. Future studies aimed at mining genomic and metagenomic datasets for sequence signatures indicative of deaminase toxin activity have the potential to provide heretofore unobtainable insights into the complexities of bacterial interactions in nature.
claims.evidence: This is speculative reasoning about future research directions.

claims.claim: Under certain circumstances hypermutator phenotypes proliferate within bacterial populations.
claims.source: There is strong evidence that under certain circumstances hypermutator phenotypes proliferate within bacterial populations (Barrick and Lenski, 2013; Mena et al., 2008; Denamur et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Barrick and Lenski, 2013; Mena et al., 2008; Denamur et al., 2000.

claims.claim: In hypermutator cells, the fitness contribution of beneficial mutations outweighs the reduction on fitness by other, deleterious mutations.
claims.source: In such cells, the fitness contribution of beneficial mutations outweighs the reduction on fitness by other, deleterious mutations (Denamur and Matic, 2006; Jayaraman, 2011).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Denamur and Matic, 2006 and Jayaraman, 2011.

claims.claim: In spatially structured, cooperating bacterial systems, hypermutator phenotypes could be transiently achieved with the aid of neighboring cells via the delivery of a mutagenic toxin.
claims.source: In spatially structured, cooperating bacterial systems, it is conceivable that such hypermutator phenotypes could be transiently achieved with the aid of neighboring cells via the delivery of a mutagenic toxin.
claims.evidence: This is speculative reasoning about the ecological role of mutagenic toxins.

claims.claim: A toxin that acts as a mutagen of a cooperating bacterium could also remain as a component of the antibacterial arsenal of the producer.
claims.source: Additionally, our data show that the same deaminase toxin can mutagenize certain bacteria while causing death in others. Therefore, a toxin that acts as a mutagen of a cooperating bacterium could also remain as a component of the antibacterial arsenal of the producer.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that DddA has different effects on different species.

claims.claim: DNA repair pathways may provide one source of diversity in determining cell fate following intoxication by DddA.
claims.source: This suggests that the determinants of cell fate following intoxication by DddA frequently vary between species. DNA repair pathways may provide one relevant source of diversity.
claims.evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on observed species differences.

claims.claim: mug orthologs are present across Enterobacteriaceae but not found in most Pseudomonads.
claims.source: Interestingly, mug orthologs are not universal among bacteria; the gene is present across Enterobacteriaceae, but it is not found in most Pseudomonads (Brunder and Karch, 2000; Silby et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is cited from Brunder and Karch, 2000 and Silby et al., 2011.

claims.claim: Recognition and turnover of DddA via cellular proteolytic machinery is one potential source of stochasticity in determining cell fate.
claims.source: Recognition and turnover of DddA via cellular proteolytic machinery is one potential source of this stochasticity. In the majority of cells belonging to a resistant species, proteolytic machinery may fortuitously and effectively deplete DddA; however, in a small subset of these cells, this machinery might fail to act before DddA installs one or more mutations.
claims.evidence: This is speculative reasoning about mechanisms of resistance.

claims.claim: Killing of target cells by interbacterial antagonistic systems can rely on the delivery of exceedingly small numbers of toxin molecules – in some cases as few as one.

results.result: DddA causes nucleoid disintegration and DNA fragmentation in E. coli through a mechanism involving cytosine deamination and base excision repair. Ung inactivation leads to uracil accumulation and alleviates nucleoid disruption, but deletions of downstream BER endonucleases (Xth, Nfo) have no effect.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C10 provide converging evidence from microscopy (C5), gel electrophoresis (C6), and fluorescent uracil labeling (C8) that DddA causes nucleoid damage through a Ung-dependent pathway. The mechanistic link to BER is established through established knowledge (C7, C51, C52) and genetic experiments showing Ung-specific effects (C9, C10). The data are internally consistent and well-controlled.

results.result: DddA causes replication fork collapse and introduces C•G-to-T•A mutations in E. coli, but Ung inactivation does not rescue cells from killing despite preventing nucleoid degradation.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C13 demonstrate that DddA kills cells through replication fork collapse (C12) independent of Ung-mediated DNA damage (C11), while simultaneously introducing mutations (C13). The use of established replication markers (DnaN-YPet) and whole genome sequencing provides strong evidence. The paradox that Ung deletion prevents nucleoid damage but not killing is well-documented.

results.result: DddA delivered via T6SS has variable effects across bacterial species: enteric bacteria and A. baumannii resist killing, while Pseudomonas and Burkholderia species are highly susceptible. DddA accounts for all T6SS inhibitory activity in sensitive species.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C16, C61-C63 provide systematic competition assay data across multiple species showing species-specific responses to DddA. The use of catalytically inactive DddA (dddAE1347A) and T6SS-deficient strains (ΔicmF) as controls strengthens the conclusions. The observation that Ung deletion does not affect P. aeruginosa susceptibility (C63) is consistent with the proposed killing mechanism.

results.result: DddA-resistant bacteria (E. coli, K. pneumoniae, EHEC) accumulate mutations during intoxication, with a 10-fold increase in rifampicin resistance frequency. Mutations are predominantly C•G-to-T•A transitions in the 5'-TC-3' context preferred by DddA, distributed randomly across the genome.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C25 provide comprehensive evidence for DddA-mediated mutagenesis through mutation frequency assays (C18, C22), rpoB sequencing (C19), whole genome sequencing (C21, C23, C24), and statistical analysis (C20, C23). The mutation signature is highly specific and significantly enriched compared to spontaneous mutations. The random distribution of mutations (C25) is well-documented. This represents a novel finding with strong supporting data.

results.result: Bacteria susceptible to DddA killing (P. aeruginosa, B. cenocepacia K56-2, B. ambifaria) do not accumulate mutations, except when Ung is inactivated. This suggests mutagenesis is rare in sensitive species but may increase when DNA repair is compromised.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C27 and C64-C66 demonstrate species-specific differences in mutagenesis outcomes. The observation that P. aeruginosa Δung shows elevated mutation frequency (C27) while wild-type does not (C26) provides strong evidence for the role of DNA repair in determining cell fate. The low frequency of DddA-signature mutations in wild-type P. aeruginosa (C65) supports the interpretation that mutagenesis is rare in sensitive species.

results.result: Mutagenic activity is a common feature of deaminase superfamily toxins. Representatives from BaDTF2 and BaDTF3 subfamilies exhibit toxicity and introduce high levels of C•G-to-T•A transitions in E. coli, each with distinct sequence context preferences.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C32 demonstrate that mutagenic activity extends beyond DddA to other deaminase toxin families. The use of bioinformatic analysis (C28), toxicity assays (C29), SNV analysis (C30), and sequence logo analysis (C31, C32) provides strong evidence. The distinct sequence preferences of each toxin family strengthen the conclusion that this is a general property of deaminase toxins.

results.result: The BaDTF2 representative SsdA preferentially targets single-stranded DNA with potent cytosine deaminating activity, can target double-stranded DNA with lower efficiency, and shows minimal activity toward RNA targets.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C37 provide comprehensive biochemical characterization of SsdA substrate specificity through in vitro deamination assays (C33-C35), poisoned primer extension assays (C36), and RNA-seq analysis (C37). The convergence of in vitro and in vivo data strengthens the conclusion that DNA is the physiologically relevant substrate.

results.result: The crystal structure of SsdA-SsdAI complex reveals that SsdA contains the core deaminase fold but bears little structural homology to characterized deaminases including DddA. BaDTF2 proteins lack conserved DYW motifs and instead contain a unique SGW motif near the active site.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C47 provide detailed structural analysis of SsdA at 3.0 Å resolution. The structure reveals both conserved deaminase features (C39) and unique characteristics (C41, C45-C47). The comparison with DYW proteins (C46-C47) and structural analysis of the immunity complex (C43-C44) are well-documented. The deposition of coordinates (C92) enables independent verification.

results.result: Despite predicted shared ancestry, DddA shows greater structural similarity to eukaryotic ssDNA-targeting deaminases (AID/APOBEC) than to SsdA, suggesting cytosine deaminases targeting ssDNA evolved at least twice from the ancestral deaminase fold.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C71 provide evolutionary insights based on structural comparisons. The inference is supported by structural data from both DddA and SsdA structures, though the conclusion is somewhat speculative. The claim is consistent with established understanding of deaminase evolution (Iyer et al., 2011) and represents a reasonable interpretation of the structural data.

results.result: DddA intoxication shares mechanistic parallels with thymineless death (TLD), including uracil incorporation into DNA, replication arrest, and chromosome degradation. In both processes, removal of uracil does not rescue cells from death.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C76 draw parallels between DddA intoxication and the established phenomenon of TLD. The comparison is supported by experimental data (C76 references Figure 2A) and established knowledge about TLD (C74-C75). However, the authors appropriately note that the precise mechanism of TLD remains unclear, limiting the mechanistic insights that can be drawn from this comparison.

results.result: DddA can install multiple mutations on a single genome during one intoxication event.
results.evaluation: Claim C89 is directly supported by whole genome sequencing data showing multiple mutations per clone (Figure 4). This observation has important implications for the evolutionary impact of deaminase toxins, as noted in the discussion.

results.result: The authors propose several speculative mechanisms for the variable effects of DddA across species, including targeting of highly transcribed regions, stochastic proteolytic degradation, and differences in DNA repair pathways.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C73, C81-C82, C83, and C85 are explicitly speculative and not directly tested in the manuscript. While these hypotheses are reasonable and grounded in the observed data, they require additional experimental validation. The authors appropriately present these as potential explanations rather than established conclusions.

results.result: DddA is a double-stranded DNA-targeting cytosine deaminase delivered via the T6SS of B. cenocepacia, which is highly toxic when expressed in E. coli and represents an unusual activity compared to other DNA-targeting deaminases.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C48-C50 establish the basic properties of DddA based on prior work (Mok et al., 2020). These claims provide essential context for the current study and are well-supported by the cited literature. The current manuscript builds on this foundation to explore the mutagenic consequences of DddA activity.

results.result: The manuscript establishes the broader context of interbacterial toxin delivery systems and deaminase enzymes, noting that while short-term effects of toxin delivery have been studied, the long-term evolutionary impact on target populations has not been explored.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C59 provide background knowledge from the literature that establishes the context and novelty of the current study. These claims are well-supported by appropriate citations and accurately represent the state of the field. Claim C57 identifies the knowledge gap that the current study addresses.

results.result: Previously characterized DYW deaminase family proteins are found in plants and protists, participate in organellar mRNA editing, and contain PPR repeats that recruit the catalytic domain to target mRNAs. Only one DYW protein has been biochemically characterized in vitro.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C68 and C91 provide established knowledge about DYW proteins from the literature. These claims are well-supported by appropriate citations and provide important context for understanding how bacterial BaDTF2 proteins differ from eukaryotic DYW proteins.

results.result: The manuscript provides various contextual observations about bacterial genetics and mutation patterns, including the distribution of dddA in B. cenocepacia strains, the distribution of mug orthologs, and the prevalence of C•G-to-T•A transitions in evolving bacterial populations.
results.evaluation: Claims C60, C84, C87-C88, and C90 provide factual context from bioinformatic analysis and literature. These claims are well-supported but represent background information rather than primary findings of the study.

results.result: The manuscript discusses the potential ecological and evolutionary implications of mutagenic toxins, including their potential to study bacterial interactions in nature and their relationship to hypermutator phenotypes.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C80 and C86 discuss potential implications and future directions. While C79-C80 and C86 are supported by literature, C78 is speculative about future research directions. These claims represent important discussion points but are not directly tested in the current study.

results.result: Structural and sequencing data from this study have been deposited in public databases (PDB: 7JTU; SRA: PRJNA659516).
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C93 document data availability. These are factual statements about data deposition that can be independently verified.
